name: Dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE)

lead: DMAE is an amino alcohol that appears in some skin-care products marketed for firming and improving skin tone. People use it hoping for tighter-looking skin and fewer visible wrinkles.

It is mainly an industrial chemical, and its bitartrate salt is sold as an oral nootropic. No mechanism for skin firming is documented, and animal work cited for it concerns memory. The only registered human study found involving a DMAE skin product tested a multi-ingredient combination.

paras: Used as a topical cream or serum ingredient, usually in a daily face-care routine, or as an oral supplement. Users of firming products typically apply them for weeks before judging results.
The pure industrial liquid is flammable and corrosive and carries hazard warnings. Safety data for cosmetic or supplement use in people are limited.

angle.text: DMAE is an ingredient in skin-firming creams marketed for a tighter, smoother look, and is also sold as an oral nootropic. The only registered human study found tested a multi-ingredient product.

lead: Dimethylaminoethanol (DMAE, also deanol, DMEA) is an ingredient in some skin-care gels and creams sold for firming and smoothing aging skin. People use it topically in the hope of tighter-looking skin, softer fine lines on the forehead and around the eyes, and a fuller lip shape.[1] It is also sold as the bitartrate salt in oral nootropic supplements.[2][3]

DMAE is an analog of choline and a precursor of acetylcholine. A 2005 review in the American Journal of Clinical Dermatology proposed that acetylcholine acts as a cytokine-like signal in skin that regulates cell proliferation, differentiation and secretion, which could underlie DMAE's cutaneous activity.[1] The review summarised a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of a 3% DMAE facial gel applied daily for 16 weeks, which reported improvements in forehead lines and fine periorbital wrinkles and in lip shape and fullness.[1]

Outside cosmetics, DMAE is mainly an industrial chemical used as a curing agent for polyurethanes and epoxy resins and as an intermediate for other compounds.[2][3] In the mid-20th century and 1970s it was also studied as a drug, including in tardive dyskinesia trials.[4][5][6]
infobox: Bitartrate salt (about 37% DMAE) in supplements; topical cosmetic ingredient[3]

paras: DMAE is a bifunctional molecule carrying a tertiary amine and a primary alcohol. It is prepared industrially by ethoxylation of dimethylamine, or by reaction of dimethylamine with ethylene oxide, and is a flammable, corrosive liquid with a fishy odour that mixes readily with water.[3][2] Wikipedia lists a boiling point of about 134 degrees Celsius and a flash point of about 39 degrees.[3] Reported oral LD50 in rats is around 1 to 2 g per kg depending on the source.[2][3]

The bitartrate salt used in supplements supplies about 37 percent DMAE by weight.[3] DMAE is also a precursor to 2-dimethylaminoethyl chloride and its acrylate ester is used as a flocculating agent.[3] Researchers studying cell membranes have used dimethylethanolamine as a substrate in phospholipid methylation experiments, as an intermediate between phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylcholine.[7]

The 2005 review describes DMAE as a choline analog and precursor of acetylcholine. It notes growing evidence that acetylcholine acts as a ubiquitous cytokine-like molecule regulating proliferation, differentiation, movement and secretion of cells in a paracrine and autocrine way, and suggests this modulatory role may contribute to DMAE's skin activity.[1]

Product marketing often describes DMAE as acting on muscle tone beneath the skin to produce a lifting effect; the published review frames the activity in terms of cell-signalling rather than muscle contraction.[1]

Animal research has examined how deanol is metabolised in rat brain and whether it affects acetylcholine synthesis, a topic cited in T Nation's supplement references.[8] Wikipedia notes animal studies suggesting possible benefit for spatial and working memory and reports no human trial results for the nootropic use.[3]

Cosmetic products use DMAE, often as the bitartrate salt at low percentage concentrations, as a skin-firming ingredient; Grokipedia describes concentrations up to about 3 percent.[2] Manufacturers and proponents describe it as tightening sagging skin and improving tone.[3] The studied form was a 3% facial gel applied daily.[1]

In the trial, the areas assessed included forehead lines, periorbital wrinkles, lip shape and fullness, under-eye dark circles, nasolabial folds, neck sagging and neck firmness, so users interested in lower-face and neck contour were among the intended audience.[1]

DMAE bitartrate is sold as an oral nootropic. Animal studies cited by Wikipedia suggest possible benefit for spatial and working memory, and a pyroglutamate form has been studied against scopolamine-induced memory deficits.[3] Deanol bitartrate also appears in stimulant-style supplement blends, such as one T Nation forum thread that lists 17 mg per serving alongside caffeine and yohimbe extract.[9]

Deanol appears in the medical literature from at least 1959 as a drug.[10] In the 1970s it was tested in tardive dyskinesia, Huntington's chorea, L-dopa-induced dyskinesia and senile dementia, with randomized trials published from 1977 to 1981.[5][6][11][12][13][14] A 1999 meta-analysis found that deanol was no more effective than placebo for tardive dyskinesia, and Cochrane reviews of cholinergic drugs for the condition covered deanol among others.[15][4][16][17]
Its cosmetic profile rose after the 2005 dermatology review that summarised the 16-week gel trial.[1]

Concentrated DMAE is classified under GHS as corrosive and acutely toxic by several routes, with hazard statements for skin burns and eye damage. This is an industrial-handling classification and does not directly describe finished cosmetic products.[3][2] Wikipedia cites a 2002 US National Toxicology Program review of its toxicological literature without summarising the findings.[3]

In the cosmetic trial, application of the 3% gel was reported as well tolerated.[1] A 1979 report on high oral doses described mood changes in 8 of 38 patients (five depressed, three hypomanic), seven of whom had histories of affective symptoms.[18]
DMAE is rarely discussed as a standalone item on appearance forums. On T Nation it appears mainly as an ingredient (deanol bitartrate) in stimulant-style and mood supplements.[9][8]

A randomized, placebo-controlled study reviewed in 2005 tested a 3% DMAE facial gel applied daily for 16 weeks. It was reported as safe and efficacious (p < 0.05) for forehead lines and periorbital fine wrinkles and for lip shape, fullness and the overall appearance of aging skin. Effects did not regress during a 2-week stop. Trends (p between 0.05 and 0.1) were seen for coarse wrinkles, under-eye dark circles, nasolabial folds, sagging neck skin and neck firmness, and application was well tolerated.[1]

A registered phase 2 study (44 participants, completed 2025) tested a serum and cream combining GABA, DMAE, cysteamine and bakuchiol for skin whitening and anti-aging; because several ingredients were combined, it does not isolate DMAE's effect.[19]

Oral deanol was studied in the 1970s and 1980s in tardive dyskinesia, with randomized trials and Cochrane reviews of cholinergic drugs covering it; a double-blind crossover trial in nine patients with Huntington's chorea reported no change in hyperkinesia. These concern movement disorders, not skin.[4][5][6][11][12] One report described mood changes in 8 of 38 patients at high oral doses.[18]

lore.intro: Community material on DMAE is mostly about its role in supplements rather than skin firming.[9]
